reply:
Meine liebe Marie,

Ich bin heute Morgen früh nach Wien zurückgekehrt, wo ich gestern Nachmittag im Prater war. Er ähnelt unserem Tiergarten, ist jedoch durch breitere Alleen geschnitten und der Boden ist grüner bedeckt. Es gibt mehrere große freie Grünflächen. Überall verteilt stehen unzählige kleine Schenken, ganz im Stil von Moabit oder Pankow, nichts wie unsere Zelte oder Hofgärtner. Man muss den Prater gesehen haben, um Wien wirklich kennenzulernen. Die Hitze ist noch da, aber die Luft ist frisch. Ich denke oft an dich und die Kinder. Gute Nacht.

Dein G.W.F. Hegel

Marie,

Am Samstag nachmittag gingen wir im Prater spazieren. Er gleicht unserem Tiergarten, ist aber mit mehr Gras bewachsen und hat weit größere freie Platten. Die Alleen sind breiter und geschnitten. Überall stehen unendlich viele Schenken, ganz im Stil von Moabit oder Pankow, nichts wie unsere Zelte oder Gärten. Man muss dort gewesen sein, um Wien wirklich zu sehen. Es war ein angenehmer Spaziergang, und ich denke oft an dich.

Dein G. W. F. Hegel

Meine liebe Marie,

gestern Nachmittag bin ich im Prater gewesen. Es ist ein Wald wie unser Tiergarten, aber die Alleen sind breiter und der Boden dichter mit Gras bedeckt. Es gibt mehrere größere freie grüne Plätze. Überall sind unzählige Buden aufgestellt, die nicht an unsere Zelte oder Hofgärtner erinnern, sondern eher den Stil von Moabit oder Pankow haben. Man muss den Prater gesehen haben, um Wien wirklich kennengelernt zu haben. Ich bin gesund und werde morgen weiterfahren.

Dein
G. W. F. Hegel

To continue my account, I finally went to the Prater on Saturday afternoon, for one is supposed to have been there if one wishes to have seen Vienna. It is a forest like our Tiergarten—intersected by avenues, with no other arrangements—the difference being that the ground is more covered with grass, there are several larger open green spaces, and the avenues are wider—an unspeakable number of beer gardens are scattered about, but not like our tents and market gardeners, rather in the style of Moabit or Pankow.

Meine liebe Marie,

Ich sitze im neuen Wirtshaus hier in Töplitz, das prächtig am „König von Preußen“ hängt. Der Weg von hier führte über Abersau nach Culm, jenem Ort, der durch die Schlacht von 1807 berühmt ist. Die Landschaft besteht aus einer Folge von Hügeln und Feldern, allesamt kultiviert und fruchtbar. Töplitz selbst liegt wunderschön und angenehm.

Sogleich nach der Ankunft stieg ich, auf Anraten der Fräulein Stok, auf den Schlackenberg gegenüber dem Haus. Man muss den Hügel umrunden, um die Aussicht zu genießen: das weite Land erstreckt sich bis zu den höheren Gebirgen, ein vielfältiger Wechsel von Hügeln, Tälern und Reihen von Häusern. Im Spitalgarten trank ich von der Quelle des Augenwassers, das mir gut tat. Danach ging ich in den Park des Schlosses des Fürsten Clary, des Herrn dieser Gegend, und nahm im Steinbad ein Bad, dessen Quelle wunderbar ist.

Ich aß mit Appetit und werde morgen zum Schloßberg reiten. Die Leute sind ordentlich und wünschen nichts Besseres, als dass man in gutem Einvernehmen mit ihnen ist. Es ist eine ruhige, wohlgeordnete Welt hier, die der Ordnung und dem Frieden huldigt.

Dein treuer Gatte
Hegel

Töplitz, den 11. Sept. 1824.

Meine liebe Marie,

die Gegend ist ganz anders als erwartet. Die Straße führt über Abersau und Culm, dem Schauplatz jener bekannten Schlacht, durch eine Folge von Hügeln und Feldern. Alles Land ist kultiviert und fruchtbar; man sieht keine Ödnis, nur die ordnungsmäßige Arbeit des Menschen. Töplitz selbst liegt schön und angenehm. Ich habe in einem völlig neuen Wirtshaus logiert, dessen Schild den König von Preußen trägt.

Sogleich ging ich auf den Schlackenberg, gerade gegenüber dem Haus, wie mir Fräulein Stok riet. Man muss um den Berg herum, um die Aussicht zu genießen, die sich über die ganze weite Gegend erstreckt. Erst begrenzen höhere Gebirgsketten den Blick; vorher wechseln Hügel, Täler und Häuserreihen ab. Im Spitalgarten trank ich von einer Quelle, die als Augenwasser gilt; sie tat mir sichtlich wohl. Danach besuchte ich den Park des Schlosses des Prinzen Clary, des Herrn dieser Gegend, und nahm ein Bad im Steinbad, dessen Quelle wunderbar ist.

Ich aß mit gutem Appetit. Die Leute sind ordentlich und scheinen nichts Besseres zu wünschen, als dass man in gutem Einvernehmen mit ihnen lebt. Morgen reite ich auf den Schloßberg.

Dein
G. W. F. Hegel

Töplitz, den 11. Sept. 1824.

Meine liebe, ich schreibe Dir von einer ganz neuen Herberge, die das Wappen des preußischen Königs zeigt. Der Weg hierher führte über Abersau und Culm, jenes Feld, wo einst die große Schlacht geschah. Die Landschaft ist eine fruchtbare, kultivierte Abfolge von Hügeln und Feldern, die sich bis zu den höheren Gebirgen erstreckt, die den Horizont abschließen. Ich machte sogleich einen Spaziergang auf den Schlackenberg, den mir Fräulein Stok empfohlen hatte. Man muß um den Hügel herum, um die weite Aussicht über die ganze Region zu genießen, mit ihrer abwechselnden Reihe von Tälern und Häuserzeilen.

Im Spitalgarten trank ich von einer Quelle, die als Augenwasser gilt; sie tat mir wohl. Dann besuchte ich den Park des Schlosses des Prinzen Clary, des Herrn dieser Gegend, und nahm ein Bad im Steinbad, dessen Quelle wunderbar ist. Ich aß mit gutem Appetit. Die Leute hier sind ordentlich und scheinen nichts Besseres zu wünschen, als mit einem in gutem Einvernehmen zu stehen. Morgen reite ich auf den Schloßberg. Bis dahin verbleibe ich Dein getreuer Hg.

Order, and they also want nothing better than that one gets along with them in order. From here it goes over Abersau), Culm — the region of the Battle of Culm, through nothing but a succession of hills and fields — all cultivated and fertile — to Töplitz, which lies very beautifully and pleasantly. I lodged in a brand-new inn (one), because its sign is to the King of Prussia. — Today immediately to the Schlackenberg, which is opposite the inn, — Miss Stok had also recommended this route to me, — on this hill one overlooks the entire region around Töplitz, i.e. if one goes around the top of the hill; — an extremely pleasant view, — the very wide region — finally bounded by higher mountain ranges, — the most varied succession of hills, valleys, rows of houses — everything is most cheerful; — then drank the spring water in the hospital garden — one spring is eye-water, which did me great good — into the park, which belongs to the palace of Prince Clary, the lord of the region — then took a bath in the stone bath — a magnificent spring — then dined with appetite — I shall drive to the castle hill. —

Meine liebe Marie,

Es ist Montag früh, der 27. September. Gestern Nachmittag hat sich das Wetter aufgeklärt, und heute ist es nicht zu heiß und verspricht, beständig zu bleiben – man könnte sagen, das schönste Wetter der Welt. Ich war den ganzen Tag auf den Beinen, zunächst in der Esterhazischen Gallerie, dann in Schönbrunn, wo ich auch zu Tisch saß. Die Müdigkeit von all dem Stehen und Gehen macht sich nun bemerkbar, doch der Geist ist wach.

Ich habe in dieser Wirbelsturm-Existenz alles gesehen und genossen, was zu sehen war. Heute besonders die Landschaft, die im strahlenden Sonnenschein schön, unendlich vielfältig und liebenswert erschien. Ich habe beschlossen, die Sehenswürdigkeiten noch einmal zu besuchen, um das Gute festzuhalten und einen Schatz der Erinnerung zu schaffen. Die italienische Oper, die in einer halben Stunde beginnt, werde ich nicht ein zweites Mal besuchen.

Ich hatte vor, am Freitag, den 1. Oktober, zu eilen, aber da du mir gestattet hast, länger zu bleiben, genieße ich die Ruhe. Ich füge diesem Blatt noch ein wenig hinzu, schreibe also trotz der Ermüdung, werde aber keine weiteren Berichte mehr geben.

Dein
G.W.F. Hegel

Wien, den 29. Septbr.

Meine Liebe, ich bin todmüde und setze mich, um dir von diesem herrlichen Tage zu erzählen. Gestern Nachmittag wurde das Wetter wieder klar, und heute ist es das schönste der Welt, nicht zu heiß und verspricht beständig zu bleiben. So konnte ich die schöne, unendlich mannigfaltige und liebliche Landschaft im prächtigen Sonnenschein genießen. Ich war den ganzen Tag auf den Beinen, in der Esterhazischen Gallerie und in Schönbrunn, wo ich auch aß. Alles habe ich im Sturmwind gesehen und genossen. Damit das Gute bewahrt bleibt und sich ein Schatz der Erinnerung bildet, will ich die sights noch einmal durchlaufen. Die italienische Oper fängt in einer halben Stunde an; ein zweites Mal werde ich sie nicht sehen. Ich hätte es am Freitag, den 1. Octbr., eilig zu dir gemacht, aber da du mir die Erlaubnis gegeben hast, länger zu bleiben, lasse ich es. Ich füge noch ein Blatt bei und schreibe ein wenig, obgleich ich müde bin. Weitere Berichte werde ich nicht mehr geben.

Dein G. W. F. Hegel

Wien, den 28. Sept.

Ich bin so müde, dass ich kaum die Feder heben kann, doch ich füge noch ein Blatt hinzu, ehe ich mich zur Ruhe lege. Gestern Nachmittags klärte sich das Wetter auf, und heute ist es das schönste der Welt, nicht zu heiß und verspricht beständig zu bleiben. Die schöne, unendlich mannigfaltige und anmutige Landschaft habe ich heute im herrlichen Sonnenschein genossen.

Den ganzen Tag war ich auf den Beinen, sowohl in der Esterhazischen Gallerie als auch in Schönbrunn, wo ich auch ein Mittagessen eingenommen habe. Ich habe in diesem Wirbelwind alles gesehen und genossen. Da die italienische Oper in einer halben Stunde beginnt, werde ich sie nicht ein zweites Mal sehen. Ich hatte vor, am 1. Oktober, einem Freitag, rasch zu Euch zu eilen, da Du mir aber die Erlaubnis gabst, länger zu bleiben, werde ich die Sehenswürdigkeiten noch einmal besuchen, um das Gute zu bewahren und einen Schatz der Erinnerung zu schaffen.

Ich werde keine weiteren Berichte mehr geben. Lebt herzlich wohl.

Euer treuer Mann

I am adding another sheet and scribbling a bit more, although I am dull and tired — from standing and walking all day in the Esterházy Gallery and in Schönbrunn, where I ate; since the Italian opera is about to begin in half an hour, I will not engage in any further reports, only that it cleared up yesterday afternoon, and today the weather is the most beautiful in the world, not too hot and promising consistency. — Flesh and blood have struggled with the will — to hasten to meet you from here on Friday, October 1st; however, you give me permission to stay longer, I have seen and enjoyed everything in the whirlwind; I have been diligent, on my feet all day, and there is still much to see; — in order to preserve the good and create for myself a treasure of memory, I must see it once more, — of course I will not see the Italian opera for a second time; the beautiful, infinitely varied, lovely countryside I have only just experienced today, and savored in what beautiful sunshine.

Meine liebe Marie,

Heute Mittag verbrachte ich den Vormittag in Ruhe und ordnete dann die Angelegenheiten des Eilwagens. Danach spazierten wir um einige Bastionen und besuchten die Schlosskapelle. Ich hörte nur einen Teil der Predigt, da ich zu weit weg saß, um viel zu verstehen, doch die schöne Sprache, das Orgelspiel und die Feierlichkeit gefielen mir. Bei der Messe war die Musik herrlich, besonders die reinen Knabenchöre. Wir sahen Kaiser und Kaiserin sehr gut. Der Kaiser hat einen sehr würdigen, schönen Kopf. Ich fragte Leute nach dem kleinen Prinzen; sie nennen ihn den kleinen Napoleon. Er hat einen schönen Knabenkopf, dunkelblondes Haar, einen ruhigen, ernsten Ausdruck und eine natürliche Haltung.

Dein G. W. F. Hegel

An meine liebe Marie,

Ich hatte heute Morgen Ruhe und ordnete die Sache mit dem Eilwagen. Nachher ging ich um einige Bastionen und besuchte die Schlosskirche. Ich hörte nur einen Teil der Predigt, da ich nicht nah genug war, um viel zu verstehen, doch die schöne Sprache, das Orgelspiel und die Andacht fielen mir auf.

Bei der Messe war die Musik vortrefflich, besonders die reinen Knabenstimmen. Den Kaiser und die Kaiserin sah ich sehr gut; der Kaiser hat einen sehr würdevollen, schönen Kopf. Ich fragte nach dem kleinen Prinzen. Man nennt ihn den kleinen Napoleon. Er hat einen schönen Knabenhaupt, dunkelblondes Haar und einen ruhigen, ernsten Ausdruck, mit natürlicher Haltung.

Dein
G. W. F. Hegel

Meine liebe, ich habe heute Vormittags geruht und den Eilwagen arrangiert. Dann bin ich um ein paar Bastionen gegangen und besuchte die Schlosskapelle. Ich hörte ein Stück einer Predigt; da ich nicht nah genug war, verstand ich wenig, aber die schöne Sprache, das Orgelspiel und die Andacht gefielen mir. Bei der Messe war die Musik herrlich, besonders die reinen Knabenstimmen. Ich sah den Kaiser und die Kaiserin sehr wohl. Der Kaiser hat einen sehr würdigen, schönen Kopf. Ich fragte die Leute nach dem kleinen Prinzen; sie nennen ihn den kleinen Napoleon. Er hat einen schönen Knabenkopf, dunkelblondes Haar, einen ruhigen, ernsten Gesichtsausdruck und eine natürliche Haltung. Ich grüße Dich herzlich.

This morning I rested, then arranged the express coach matter, after which I took a walk for a few bastions, then went into the castle chapel, where I heard part of a sermon, though not close enough to understand much, only noticing beautiful language, organ, and decorum, then attended the mass, where there was beautiful music, especially from the pure boys' voices, and what is the main thing, saw the Emperor and the Empress very well; the former is indeed a very dignified, handsome head, also the little Napoleon, as the people called him, whom I asked about the little Prince, a handsome boy's head, dark blonde hair, calm and serious, and natural bearing.

Meine liebe Marie,

Der neue Bassist hier ist ein vortrefflicher Buffo, und auch das neue Ensemble in *Il barbiere di Siviglia* gefiel mir. Ich nahm, wie gewohnt, in der vorderen Reihe Platz. Neben mir saß ein Perser oder Türke, den der Intendant als Prinz Ipsilanti vorstellte – eine Figur, die mir gänzlich unbekannt ist. Ich grüßte ihn höflich, worauf er mir mit einer Geste an Stirn und Brust dankte. So klatschten wir dann gemeinsam und kräftig, was die Abendstimmung angenehm machte.

Dein G. W. F. Hegel

Meine liebe Marie,

Der Opernbesuch heute war recht unterhaltsam. Ein neuer Bassist vom besten Buffo-Typ erschien und gab in „Der Barbier von Sevilla“ eine bemerkenswerte Vorstellung. Einige der Frauen auf der Bühne sind Deutsche. Ich nahm, wie ich konnte, Platz in der ersten Reihe.

Mein Nachbar war ein Perser oder Türke, der offenbar jeden Abend denselben Stuhl besetzt. Der Intendant nannte ihn Prinz Ipsilanti, wovon ich freilich nichts weiß. Ich grüßte ihn höflich, worauf er mir dankbar Stirn und Brust berührte. Wir klatschten dann eifrig zusammen.

Dein
G. W. F.

Meine liebe Marie,

Hier sah ich gestern einen neuen Bassisten, ein vortrefflicher Buffo war er, und auch ein neuer Künstler trat in Figaros Hochzeit auf. Mehrere der Damen sind Deutsche. Ich suche mich, wenn es geht, in die erste Reihe zu setzen. Gestern saß ich neben einem Perser oder Türken, der jeden Abend denselben Platz einnimmt. Der Direktor sagte, es sei der Prinz Ipsilanti, wenngleich ich nicht weiß, wer das ist. Ich grüßte ihn, und er dankte mir, indem er Stirn und Brust kreuzte. Darauf klatschten wir beide kräftig zusammen.

Dein H.

A new bassist, an excellent type of buffo, appeared here, and a new one also emerged from this thicket in The Barber of Seville, but the several ladies are German. — I go to the front row if possible and sat here next to a Persian or Turk, who sits in the same place every evening — the manager said: it is Prince Ipsilanti, which I do not know. I greeted him, he thanked me by crossing his forehead and chest, — we clapped together vigorously.

It is about my birthday that I have to tell. The remembrance you sent me, which Mrs. Aimée prepared—very nicely—behind the scenes, just as the letters from the young people did, pleased me greatly, and I greeted and kissed you most intimately in the image of my soul. Although Mrs. Aimée had gotten up early and taken care to show me yours first, she was not up early enough. For we had already begun to celebrate this, my birthday, from its very first origin, at midnight at 12 o'clock. I was at Mr. Bloch's at a game of whist, which, very delayed and accompanied by an equally prolonged supper, brought about the blowing of the whistle for the 27th by the night watchman, which was answered and outdone by the clinking of glasses. Your health was especially toasted by me and by all (the Zelters were present), but particularly by Rösel, with heartfelt participation.

Ah! I could write so much more, also about my perhaps merely hypochondriacal pedantry, with which I insisted so much on the difference between contentment and happiness — which is also again so useless — that I swore to you and to myself that your happiness shall be the dearest thing I have. — It is also much that only passes away, is forgotten, and is undone by not being touched. This too: I was long in doubt whether I should write to you, because everything one writes or speaks depends again solely on the explanation, or because I feared it, since it is so dangerous once it has come to explaining — but I have also overcome this fear and hope everything from your mind, as it receives this written. Farewell until today’s unclouded reunion, dear Marie — only this I would like to be able to tell you yet, what feeling, how much — my existence, as much as it is — lies in these words: dear Marie. Your Wilhelm.

The other matter is that the local L. Comm. and the Rectorates are to report on the filling of the philological professorship; a domestic official in the ecclesiastical or school department is to be named for this. What do you say to this, if I take the heart in both hands and offer myself for it? — namely, actually insofar as I become Professor of Philosophy, I would also want to read philological lectures for as long as that lasts! It would be strange if I obtained a position or its salary, which you ought to have claimed for Ludwig by God and right. — I intend to write to Mr. von Zentner about this as well. — A motive I can use is that the vacancy of my local position for professors at the Realinstitut, who are to be provided for — or also for others, if restrictions are to be made at the Gymnasiums regarding the professorship of philosophical preparatory sciences — or generally. Kanne, who is the best philologist here, would do strange things at the university in another respect... It is a pity that, as I hear, Paulus with Martin and Fries has also compromised himself with the matter of freedom and therefore can probably only appear discreetly. — Schubert found a good gift in Ludwigslust — the Hereditary Grand Duke and the entire court of Schranzen following behind, he found upon his arrival — become Catholic! — Also a sign of the times. The Ludw. Tiek, Dr. Möllers’ sister, is and operates there. Your H.

For the autumn, my works for my lectures may also have acquired a more popular and condescending form and better qualified themselves for the tone of a general textbook and gymnasium instruction, for I feel myself more condescending every year, especially this year since I am a married man. — At the same time, it seems more and more with each year that in the gymnasium there was already almost too much philosophical instruction; — that now, because of religion, an hour is dropped does something; meanwhile, there is still almost a bit more of the good than would be necessary). — I certainly know at the same time that according to the Most High Decrees the instruction is to consist partly or chiefly in practical exercises; but how speculative thinking is to be practiced practically, of that I have no clear idea; already to practice abstract thinking practically is most difficult; then the empirical, because of its manifoldness, scatters the most; — it is like learning to read; one cannot begin to read whole words at once — as super-clever pedagogues have wanted — but must begin with the abstract, the individual strokes; so in thinking, in logic, it is precisely the most abstract that is the easiest, for it is quite simple, pure, and unmixed; only gradually can one proceed to thinking exercises on the sensible or concrete, when those simple sounds have properly fixed themselves in their differences. — It occurs to me in this connection that a few days ago I read an excellent third chapter of a school plan for the people's schools, which is the third to the preceding ones, as the Lord Christ came as the third man to the buyers and sellers in the temple. Equally excellent are the explanations, which I truly call classical. Thank God! that plain human reason and the earnestness of really learning something may finally break through. — Mr. von Zlentner!] is, as I see from the newspapers, back; — soon, then, the decision regarding Erlangen is to be expected, namely that it will be postponed again... Your Royal

Above all, I must testify in this my reply to you, dearest friend, how greatly I have been pleased by your so heartfelt sympathy at the happy change in my situation; I have to thank you for more than just this sympathy, for you are the creator of this part of my happiness as well; on the whole—with a few still desirable modifications deducted—I have reached my earthly goal, for with an office and a beloved wife one is finished in this world; these are the main articles of what one has to strive for for one's individual self; the rest are no longer separate chapters, but perhaps only paragraphs or footnotes. Of the weeks of my marriage so far, I will, and in fact have nothing more extensive to write; you have given me the deadline for my reply that it should occur only before the end of the honeymoon, but you yourself suppose that one does not worry about the end of it during it. I mean, however, that, having entered it with calmer views and having lived through the time from the wedding on with fewer illusions, a not distant degree of satisfaction for the rest, especially the same intimacy of trust, can be maintained. — However it may be, my greatest wish, since you were not in person—although represented and present to our spirit—at our wedding, is that you soon visit us here with the best of women; do not delay long in giving me the cheerful consciousness of having finally gotten so far that I can have you lodging with me.

Regarding your kind communications about the conditions there, insofar as they may concern me, I have found in them confirmation of what I had feared. You have indeed been kind enough to express that you still have great hope for me, but at the same time it seems that the condition has been added as a sine qua non that I must be reconciled with Jakobi, that I must do something on my part, which, however delicately the phrasing may be, I must fear can only be a "pater peceavi!" You know that you have absolute authority over me; but I am convinced that you will spare me this; you yourself state that Jakobi's relationship to me is more a pain than an opinion, the latter of which, if it were the only issue, is capable of change, but the former hardly so, and without transferring it to me, without receiving fiery coals on my head, which I would even help to place there myself.

I can say this in favor of accepting the proposal regarding the newspaper; I can add that this work allows a period during which I can continue my scholarly work, whereas any other position, such as a teaching post, would restrict me much more in this regard. Against this stands the fact that this work cannot be regarded as a solid establishment, but especially that the isolated independence is so tempting, whereas everyone must stand in connection with the state and in work for it, and the satisfaction one believes to find in private life is nevertheless deceptive and insufficient. — I will partly not lead a private life, for there is no more public person than a newspaper writer, and literary works are precisely something public; — both, of course, are not an office.

An old acquaintance, who is traveling to Munich and will take the liberty of presenting himself to you, gives me the opportunity to bring myself into a sweet remembrance with you, and to be able to wish you, dearest friend, a happy New Year. Since I have only as much time as is necessary to do this, I must refrain from adding anything else about scholastic or congress-related matters, except that the common predicate: necessary, would perhaps have to be given to their progress. It is a new, eternally memorable experience that the peoples are now making, what their princes are capable of when they themselves come together and, with personal spirit and mind, deliberate on the welfare of their peoples and of the world, and indeed according to the noblest expressed principle of universal justice and the well-being of all. For centuries, one has only seen cabinets act, or individual men who acted for themselves against others; but the present phenomenon is unique and demands a brilliant result.... Your sincere Hgl.

But what hindered me even more from a quicker reply was the desire to write a thorough judgment on the work you sent me, for which I thank you very much, and to show you at least that I have fully grasped your ideas. But I had no time for a thorough study of them — only to the extent that I have grasped the main ideas, I see in it a completion of the science that will give us the most fruitful results — I see in it the work of a mind whose friendship I can be proud of, and which will make its great contribution to the important revolution in the system of ideas of all of Germany. To encourage you to fully carry out your system would be an insult, since an activity that has seized upon such a subject does not need it. From the Kantian system and its highest completion I expect a revolution in Germany, which will proceed from principles that already exist and only need to be generally worked out and applied to all previous knowledge. Of course, such a philosophy will always remain esoteric; the idea of God as the absolute I will belong to it. In a newer study of the postulates of practical reason I had had premonitions of what you explained clearly to me in your last letter, what I found in your work, and what will finally unlock for me the foundation of Fichte’s Science of Knowledge — through the consequences that will result from it, some gentlemen will one day be set in astonishment. One will be dizzy at this highest height, by which man is so greatly elevated, but why did we come so late to the idea of valuing human dignity more highly, of recognizing his capacity for freedom, which places him in the same order of spirits? I believe there is no better sign of the times than this, that humanity is presented as so worthy of respect in itself; it is proof that the nimbus around the heads of the oppressors and gods of the earth is disappearing. The philosophers prove this dignity, the peoples will learn to feel it, and their rights, humbled in the dust, will not demand them, but will take them back themselves — appropriate them.

Religion and politics have played under one roof; the former has taught what despotism wanted: contempt for the human race, and its inability to be anything good by itself. With the spread of ideas about how everything ought to be, the indolence of the established people, who always take everything as it is, will disappear. The enlivening power of ideas—even if they still have limitations in themselves, such as those of the fatherland, its constitution, and so on—will elevate the minds, and they will learn to sacrifice for them, whereas at present the spirit of constitutions has made a pact with self-interest and has founded its realm upon it. I always call out to myself from the course of life: “Strive toward the sun, friends, so that the salvation of the human race may soon ripen! What do the hindering leaves, what do the branches want? Fight your way through to the sun, and if you tire, so much the better! It is easier to sleep!”

To Mr. M. Schelling in Tübingen, free to Schaffhausen. My dear! The delay in my reply is due partly to various business matters and partly to distractions caused by the political celebrations held here. Every ten years, the sovereign council and the approximately 90 members who have departed during this period are replenished. I cannot describe to you how human it all proceeds, or how all the intrigues at princely courts through cousins and uncles are nothing compared to the combinations made here—the father appoints his son or the son-in-law who brings the largest dowry, and so on. To learn what an aristocratic constitution is like, one must have spent such a winter before Easter, when the replenishment takes place, here.

I am writing to you because I have heard that you have now arrived at your fixed place, and I first acknowledge receipt of your letter to me, which you wrote from Stuttgart shortly before your departure for Munich. I need not tell you how much your appointment, which is also very honorable in every respect, has pleased me. Jena, bereft of so many great men, has missed you particularly, and even among the common people your loss was considered the most significant, just as the people who do not call themselves common seemed to wish to possess you again.

You will have heard into which little streams your philosophical current divides here; I, too, have started reading again, and am getting along with it better than usual. The literary gazette now about to appear will become as common an institution as the previous one and any other; it was of no further concern to Goethe; since Eichstedt offered himself and money, the whole matter was handed over to him without further ado, so that Jena might have a literary gazette. Among the new developments is the fact that Ritter has been requested by the students to lecture on galvanism; he has bypassed the philosophical faculty and awaits a decision from the courts. — Fernow could find no auditorium large enough for those who were signing up; it is said that he reads Kantian definitions to them. — As for literary news, nothing has come to my attention except a scrap from Kotzebue, *Expectorationes*, a diarrhea which he still let loose in Germany); it is the old song about Goethe and the Schlegels; the anecdote is also used therein that the former, like Friedrich! with the Hores in the journal *Deutschland* dealt uncleanly with them /), at a dinner at Loder’s swore that these people should never set foot in Jena. — Goethe is very much set on the real and on apparatuses, not only did he have Schelvern set up a botanical cabinet, but a physiological one is also being established, and from Ritter he immediately demanded the

Other needs and circumstances will be communicated to you in part by Paulus, and in part by my most humble report to you. — P. has lodged me in the front house — the parson’s residence above the classrooms — also to allow the old, good Schenk the comfort of his change of residence. Please keep the room I am currently occupying; do you not consider it expedient for supervision purposes to move the Progymnasium to this building as well, and to relocate the Realinstitut elsewhere? Mr. v. Joli) now also has his standing quarters here; she will move here in the next few days and sends you, as well as the best of ladies, her warmest greetings. I have not yet seen Mrs. v. Siebein. — Please make my very best and most friendly recommendations to the best of ladies, and likewise greet Julius, who is probably also at the Progymnasium. Your devoted Hgl. Prof. Heller‘) asked me to convey his regards to you on this occasion. You have provided us with a fine acquisition in him, both in his own right and in contrast to the customary Nuremberg slowness. If you could arrange for a number of copies of the Normatives to be sent here for sale, this would be very important for publicizing the new course of study among the local public, which still has very little knowledge of it.

If I may express a wish, it would be for a few more hours of physics—without, however, taking time away from another subject; though this might perhaps be arranged in connection with the physico-technical institute. In general, however, it is still too early to speak of it. My thoughts on the matter in general would be to equip a gymnasium richly with apparatus for this purpose, so that young people, at the age when the non-theoretical observation of these phenomena and their applications to various games is still appropriate, can soon be done with it; whereas for the university, almost nothing of such apparatus should be allowed, because the scientific and mathematically treated theory of it requires almost nothing of the kind and is suitable for the university alone.

The long delay in answering your several kind letters, dearest friend, I could only partly excuse with the generally inexcusable manner in which I am accustomed to handle letter writing. However, part of the postponement is due to my intention to thank you more extensively for the kind gift of your writing. I would indeed have found the time, measured by the clock, but not enough leisure; a letter, if it does not concern a formal business matter, becomes for me a kind of journey to the friend, and in order to be able to allow myself such a journey, I want to wait for a mind free from other activities, cares, and distractions; so I often do not get around to answering dearer letters, such as yours, before the holidays, although in my thoughts I have answered them all winter long. An illness has also had its share in the delay; and let the first thing be for me to express my heartfelt thanks for your loving invitation, which you make to me in that connection, to spend some months with you; could it be so well with me that I could carry that out! Yet my health is generally getting better again, so that I am able to attend to my office, and spring will, I hope, do its part to finally consolidate it. That you and your worthy family, including the grandson, are in good health, I take with interest from your letters.

Your preface must have interested me particularly in this respect, personally, in that I find in it the satisfaction that you approve of the path of speculative cognition that I have taken, and indeed that you undertake the commitment to work in this field and to grace us with the fruits of your meditations. The point to which you carry your presentation has been doubly interesting to me. Since this point is of the greatest interest in itself, it may also be the point in which will fall what you designate by the name of our differences. But if the path that we are to walk together is so long, and if it offers so much in common in spirit and content, then those differences seemed to me, on the scientific side, to lie in such a wide distance of conception, that for the present I hold fast to the feeling of your loving friendship, and find in it intimate satisfaction, and at the close I ask for its preservation, as I am, with all my heart, yours, Hegel.

to the Royal Danish Steward, Mr. von Thaden, in Flensburg. As I first return the friendly and heartfelt greeting with equal friendliness and heart, which you, very highly esteemed Sir, already offered me a year ago, the next thing must be to say something about why I have let this return stand so long. Look for the cause in nothing else than in the desire not to answer your friendly participation in my philosophical endeavors with a letter that is, so to speak, devoid of deeds.

I see from this that the need for philosophy is once again drawing closer to the higher authorities and that I, too, have not been forgotten. A professorship at a university is the position I have longed for again for a long time. Such a position is, according to our customs, the almost indispensable condition for giving philosophy wider entry and dissemination, as it also provides the only form of lively face-to-face interaction, which in turn exerts a completely different influence on the literary form than mere conception, and I expect from this side a greater possibility to accomplish something more satisfactory in writings.

That it was you who, as you write, caused the delay in the execution of the decrees, I shall not flatter myself on one hand, for this vanity led to nothing at least, but on the other hand I wish that it had not been me, because if it had been me, I would have been the one to cause a new undertaking in addition to the troubles I have caused you. Paulus writes to me today with yesterday’s date that I shall now have the official documents from Nuremberg in hand; however, I do not yet have them; Stutzmann will arrive here in eight days, and then I can depart for there without any embarrassment; the curriculum, Paulus writes, has not yet arrived there; before its arrival, no official activity will be required of me, as it could only consist of taking over fragmentarily for a few days the school of the old Rector, consisting of 5 to 6 students, in its old form. Even after the arrival of the curriculum, at least a few days will be necessary, for the teacher of the philosophical preparatory sciences more than for others, who have a specific plan and thread in an author, but also for these—to survey their half-yearly syllabus in advance. — I also know nothing yet, neither about the philosophical subjects or sciences that are to be taught at a Gymnasium, nor about the books that are to serve as guides, nor whether my instruction will be assigned to different classes, and thus be different, as I must almost fear from the stipulation in Klein’s local appointment.

To Your High Reverence, Mr. Senior School Councillor Dr. Niethammer in Munich. If you call me a friend of little faith, then you yourself did not intend to call me little-faithful in relation to you, dearest friend, and likewise do not take it amiss if I am little-faithful toward a certain thing, in which you do not, like the thistle heads, the Spinotzists, represent man in general as a portion of seawater separated in a bottle floating in the ocean, but rather move actively in it as in an element, which everywhere recedes where you penetrate, but which, by its very nature, also immediately closes up again, and for individual moments can rise to the surface. — Whether I such an individual moment of

They told it to God, to the earth, even to Gusmann); I hear that the reply came back today, they found deaf ears. It has been written here from Munich that you have become a Church Councillor, and moreover the first one; is there any truth in this? I hope and wish that the prospect of living together with you on the scientific earth, in Elysium, should not be blocked by a gilded partition, a partition that for you would be nothing but a shining prison.

Dear dear Refugee! It was on September 24 that instinct led me to the distressed straw widow to collect the little sheet you had prepared for me. I greeted your flower-crowned portrait with heartfelt friendship, congratulated you on the happy outcome of your journey, and thanked you for your kind remembrance and its source, as well as for the notes provided from Munich. I spent 5–6 days in old cordial friendship with Schelling in Carlsbad (where I came on the tour through Töplitz, Prague, then Weimar, — to the eighty-year-old youth, — Jena). In Prague, please do not fail to visit Professor of History, von Henniger (pronounced: Hennigahr), a brother-in-law of my uncle there and aunt here), Broad Street, Schlichting’s house, whom I have announced you to, — he is by his own inclination very willing to help you in every way with researches and materials for your works. Please give him, and then also to Librarian Hanka, my best regards; it will be of interest to you to set aside a few days for Prague. The King has given a copy of your work to Count Waldstein as a gift. Farewell, soon a happy return, which the other vacant colleagues will also effect one after another. — Today the return of Madame Crelinger (in Gabriele) is to be celebrated, if it is not a beginning of the end (Vienna is said to have been very hard on her). Your faithful Hegel.

The main thing is that the departure of the entire manuscript will infallibly take place from me this week... Regarding my journey to you, the times do not permit it, much as I would like to accept your kind invitation; — the lectures are to begin on October 13th, or perhaps on the 20th; it will not amount to much, but independently of that, I would expose myself to the danger of not being able to return, or perhaps not even being able to come to you. — The mail coach is easily sent back earlier or delayed, compared to the riding post; so that if I were to deliver the manuscript, it might easily delay my arrival more than if it were sent by the riding post. — But the war has not yet broken out; the present moment seems decisive); in a few days, peace winds may blow just as strongly, and then I will not fear the October zephyr, and will travel to you.

I am writing to you, highly esteemed friend, for a twofold reason. First, I did not tell you the exact arrangement of the copies that you were kind enough to take with you; which I wish to supply now. Of the three bound copies, one on wove paper is for Goethe, the one on writing paper for Privy Councillor Voigt, and the other on wove paper is intended for you. Of the three unbound copies, you were kind enough to send one to Frommann; as you know, the time did not allow for having them bound or cased. Furthermore, I ask you to return the other two unbound copies; in exchange, I will enclose here an order for two printed copies to Frommann, which Göbhardt will send me today. You are to be kind enough to have one sent to M. v. Knebel and the other to Seebeck.

The reason for the present letter lies in your kindness toward me in general, as well as toward my brother-in-law, to whom you were so friendly and helpful during his stay in Munich. He has applied for artillery service for several months now. The lameness mentioned in your letter, which can be found both outside and inside the walls, now receives a vigorous spur in the flanks and sharp thorny bushes under the buttocks through the dispatches from Lyon, etc.; but unfortunately, the drastic power of such a stimulant directs itself in all other directions, just not in the desired one, and the lameness might first transition into a complete stroke and catalepsy of interest in sciences and scientific institutes, since I, like every other professor, schoolteacher, and section councilor, would have to take up the rifle on my shoulder if the matter were to become serious, which I do not believe at the moment, and cannot believe, even if the eagles were planted on the walls of Paris. — What could I therefore write about particular hopes and wishes that I might have had, especially now; until now, not, for the simple reason that there was simply nothing else to write, — as I generally find that reasons, especially non-events and non-fates, are very simple; yet I have reason to believe that it has not been decided negatively either. We all recommend ourselves most heartily. Your H.
